Why the Brain Starts at the Commercial Line

The Build OrderPart 2

By lowob · 15 June 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 9-minute read · Revenue

Start the brain where you can count what it changed within a quarter. In most mid-size firms that is the commercial line: sales, marketing and account management. Commercial decisions recur weekly, resemble each other, show their outcome within months and have a budget holder who must defend them, and they already sit on a structured system: the CRM. The firm-wide knowledge base, the most common alternative, delivers value that is real but rarely measurable, which makes it hard to fund twice.

When a company decides to build its brain, two starting points usually compete. One is the firm-wide knowledge base: every methodology, template and past deliverable, searchable by anyone. It addresses a real complaint, because new staff spend weeks asking where things are. The other is the commercial line: the accounts, the pitches, the pipeline and the follow-ups that keep slipping.

Both address real pain. Only one lets a sponsor say, at the end of a quarter, what the build was worth. That difference decides whether the second phase gets funded.

The knowledge-base trap

A firm-wide knowledge base is useful in the way a good filing system is useful: everyone benefits a little, and nobody can say by how much. It is also the use case that broad assistant rollouts most resemble, and the adoption record is sobering. Fewer than 4.5% of Microsoft 365's roughly 450 million commercial customers pay for Copilot, and only 20% to 30% of those who pay open it in a typical week, according to figures Windows Latest reported in July 2026. An assistant that can see everything but has no particular job tends to become an expensive search box.

There is a second, structural problem. A knowledge base collects documents. Documents tell a system what is true; decisions tell it what the company does. In A loop with good context we described the precedent an experienced person carries (three similar past cases, what was decided, what went wrong) and noted that it is retrievable only if someone recorded it. A knowledge base built first almost never captures it.

The test: where judgment arrives first

We have published a test for where a decision layer starts to earn its keep. Judgment arrives first in decisions that are frequent, similar, quickly graded, and later defended by someone with budget or regulatory accountability (Where judgment arrives first). Run the commercial line through it.

Commercial decisionFrequencySimilar to past cases?Outcome known withinWho defends it
Qualify or drop an inbound leadDailyYesWeeksHead of sales
Pursue or pass on a pitchWeeklyMostlyOne sales cyclePartners or leadership
Approve a discount beyond standardWeeklyYesOne sales cycleFinance and sales
Set or shift campaign spendMonthlyMostlyA quarterBudget holder
Record why a deal was lostWeeklyYesAlready knownHead of sales
Prioritise accounts for the quarterQuarterlyMostlyA quarterRevenue leader

Almost every row passes on all four counts. Now run a typical knowledge-base decision through the same test: "which version of the methodology document is canonical" happens rarely, varies each time, has no clear outcome and no budget holder defending it. It is a worthwhile decision, but it belongs in a disciplined record people read, not in a system expected to learn.

Where the recoverable time actually is

The commercial line also has unusually well-documented slack. Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals found that sellers spend about 40% of their time selling, with the rest consumed by administration, data entry, research and internal coordination. Sellers already using agents expect them to cut prospect research time by about a third and email drafting time by a similar share, and top-performing sellers were 1.7 times more likely than underperformers to use agents for prospecting.

Those are vendor-run figures and expected rather than measured savings, so we treat them as direction rather than proof. But they point to the same tasks where agents are most reliable today: research, preparation, record hygiene and first drafts. The brain's first job on the commercial line is to return that time without adding risk.

You already own the store

The commercial line has a structured home that most other functions lack: the CRM. It holds accounts, contacts, stages, owners and dates. That matters because the brain needs somewhere to write outcomes back, and a closed-won or closed-lost deal is exactly that link, already sitting in a field.

The store is rarely in good shape. Validity's 2025 survey of 602 CRM users and administrators found 37% reporting revenue lost as a direct result of poor data quality, and its 2026 survey of 500 marketers found only 21% considered their CRM data very well prepared for the AI tools they use or plan to use. That is an argument for starting here, not against it. Cleaning the store is part of the build, and it pays for itself in forecasting and follow-up even before any agent is switched on. Part 4 covers how.

Where the money is going

Spending patterns point the same way. Menlo Ventures estimates that more than half of the $37bn companies spent on generative AI in 2025 went to applications rather than infrastructure, and that departmental spending reached $7.3bn, led by coding. Buyers are paying for software that does a job in a function they can measure. A brain that begins by doing a commercial job is easier to buy, easier to evaluate and easier to fund a second time than one that begins as general infrastructure.

Start where you can say, after one quarter, what moved. If you cannot, you started in the wrong place.

The case against starting here

The argument has limits, and we would rather name them than leave a reader to find them.

Regulated firms. In banking, insurance and healthcare, the first decisions that must be defended are often compliance decisions. A supervisor may ask the firm to reconstruct why a pricing exception was granted or a client communication sent. There, the decision record and audit trail come before any commercial agent. The order bends but the logic holds: start where decisions are defended.

Long enterprise sales cycles. If a deal takes eighteen months, the "quickly graded" test fails. The workaround is leading indicators (meetings held, stage progression, stakeholder coverage) chosen with care, because a system optimises whatever proxy it is given.

Service-led firms. Where the client relationship lives in delivery rather than in sales, the commercial line may run through account management and renewals. Start there; the reasoning is the same.

Very small teams. Below about ten people, the record may be a shared document and a weekly review rather than a system. Our scale guide, The scale ladder, describes what to build at each size.

Illustrative example: choosing the starting point
Decision
Build on the commercial line first and schedule the firm-wide knowledge base for after Gateway 3.
Reason and owner
Commercial decisions pass all four tests and already have a system of record; the knowledge base has no agreed success measure. Agreed by leadership; owned by the head of operations.
What changed
The knowledge base becomes a later phase with its own measure (time to first billable work for new hires) rather than the first spend.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size advisory firm, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Start where you can count the change. If nothing measurable moves in a quarter, the starting point was wrong.
  • Test decisions, not departments. Frequent, similar, quickly graded and defended decisions are where a brain learns first.
  • Clean the store as part of the build. Poor CRM data costs revenue on its own; fixing it is the first return.
  • Know when the order bends. Regulated firms record first; long cycles need careful leading indicators.
Gateway card

Before you commit to a starting point

  • The five most frequent commercial decisions listed
  • For each: how often, how similar, how soon graded, who defends it
  • One measure that will move within a quarter
  • The CRM's current data quality estimated, honestly

Common questions

Where should a company start its enterprise AI build?

Usually on the commercial line, because its decisions are frequent, similar, graded within months and defended by a budget holder, and because the CRM already provides a structured record to write outcomes into.

Why not start with a company-wide knowledge base?

A knowledge base delivers diffuse value that is hard to measure, and it captures documents rather than decisions. It is a better second or third phase than a first one.

How much time do salespeople spend selling?

Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals found sellers spend about 40% of their time selling, with the remainder on administration, research and data entry.

When should a company not start with sales and marketing?

In regulated sectors where compliance decisions must be reconstructed first, in businesses with very long sales cycles, and where the client relationship sits in delivery rather than sales.

List your five most frequent commercial decisions. How many have a written record of why they went the way they did? If the answer is none, that is where the build should begin.
